hints: Start from the $\text{COOH}$ group which must be present in both isomers, then think how the remaining three carbons can be arranged in two different carbon skeletons.
Try one isomer with a straight chain of four carbons in total, and the second with a branched chain where a methyl group is attached to the middle carbon.
walkthrough:
Fix the functional group first**
Both molecules must be carboxylic acids with formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$. That means each one ends in $\text{COOH}$. Once you fix that, you have used one carbon, so you only need to arrange the other three carbons in different ways.

Build the straight chain isomer**
Join the three remaining carbons in a straight line to the $\text{COOH}$ carbon. You get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. Count: four carbons, eight hydrogens, two oxygens. This is butanoic acid.

Build the branched chain isomer**
Now branch the skeleton. Attach two methyl groups to the carbon next to $\text{COOH}$. You get $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}$, which is 2-methylpropanoic acid. The molecular formula is unchanged but the carbon chain is branched, so these two are chain isomers.

hints: Remember an ester is $\text{RCOO}\text{R}'$, so split the four carbons between the acid side and the alcohol side in different ways while keeping the total at four.
Try one ester with one carbon on the alcohol side and three on the acid side, and a second with two carbons on each side.
walkthrough:
See esters as joined acid plus alcohol**
Think of an ester as $\text{acid part} + \text{alcohol part} - \text{H}_2\text{O}$. For $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$ you must share four carbons between the $\text{COO}$ acid fragment and the alkyl group from the alcohol.

Make two different splits**
If methanol ($\text{C}_1$) joins propanoic acid ($\text{C}_3$) you get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_3$. If ethanol ($\text{C}_2$) joins ethanoic acid ($\text{C}_2$) you get $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. If propan-1-ol ($\text{C}_3$) joins methanoic acid ($\text{C}_1$) you get $\text{HCOOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Check why they are positional isomers**
All contain the same $\text{COO}$ ester group, but the position of that group within the four carbon framework moves. Pick any two of the three above for your pair.

Final answer: Any two of:
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_3$ (methyl propanoate)
$\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (ethyl ethanoate)
$\text{HCOOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (propyl methanoate)

hints: Work backwards from your chosen ester by splitting it at the $\text{COO}$ linkage to identify which carboxylic acid and which alcohol it came from.
Recall what catalyst and heating method drives the reversible esterification equilibrium toward the ester.
walkthrough:
Match the ester to its parents**
Split your ester at the $\text{C-O}$ single bond of $\text{COO}$. The $\text{CO}$ side gains $\text{OH}$ to become the acid, the $\text{O}$ side gains $\text{H}$ to become the alcohol. For example, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ comes from $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Add the catalyst and heat**
Esterification is slow and reversible, so warm with a few drops of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (or concentrated $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$) which acts as a catalyst and dehydrating agent. Heating under reflux pushes the reaction toward the ester.

Final answer: Reagents: correct matching pair, e.g. propanoic acid + methanol for $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_3$, or ethanoic acid + ethanol for $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, or methanoic acid + propan-1-ol for $\text{HCOOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$
Conditions: concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or concentrated $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$, with heat / warm / reflux

hints: Focus only above $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and look for the very strong sharp dip near $1700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ in the ester spectrum that is missing in X.
Use the clue that X decolourises bromine water to predict which bond must appear in X but not in the ester, and where it absorbs.
Compare the region above $3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ in the two spectra and think which broad absorption shows hydrogen bonding in X.
walkthrough:
Spot the ester carbonyl**
Look above $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ at the ester spectrum. There is a very strong, sharp dip at about $1740 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. That is the classic $\text{C=O}$ stretch of an ester, expected at 1710 to 1750 $\text{ cm}^{-1}$. Now look at X in the same place. There is no sharp dip there, so X has no $\text{C=O}$. That fits the information that X is not an ester or an acid.

Explain the alkene evidence in X**
X decolourises bromine water, so X must contain a $\text{C=C}$ double bond. In the IR, X shows absorption at 1500 to 1680 $\text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C=C}$ stretching. The ester spectrum has no significant peak there, as a saturated ester has no $\text{C=C}$.

Explain the alcohol evidence in X**
Compare the high wavenumber end. The ester has only small $\text{C-H}$ dips near $3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. X has a very broad, strong dip centred around $3300 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. That broad shape is characteristic of hydrogen bonded $\text{O-H}$, at 3200 to 3650 $\text{ cm}^{-1}$ for an alcohol. So X is likely an unsaturated alcohol, which accounts for formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$ without being an acid or ester.

Final answer: Ester shows a strong sharp peak at 1710 to 1750 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C=O}$ stretch, absent in X.
X shows a peak at 1500 to 1680 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C=C}$ (alkene), absent in ester, consistent with decolourising bromine water.
X shows a broad peak at 3200 to 3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to alcohol $\text{O-H}$ stretch, absent in ester.
